items.title: RBI — Establishment, Structure & Functions
items.body:
## In one line

The **Reserve Bank of India** is India's central bank — it issues currency, sets monetary policy and regulates banks. It is asked because APPSC Prelims regularly tests its founding year, legal basis and core functions.

## Establishment

- The **Reserve Bank of India Act was passed in 1934**; the RBI **began operations on 1 April 1935**, and was **nationalised on 1 January 1949**.
- Headquartered in **Mumbai**; the current Governor (Sep 2026) is **Sanjay Malhotra**.

## Organisational structure

- Governed by a **Central Board of Directors** appointed by the Government of India for a **four-year term**.
- Full-time officials: a **Governor and not more than four Deputy Governors**; plus 10 government-nominated directors and 4 from local boards (Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Delhi).

## Core functions

| Function | What it means |
|---|---|
| Monetary authority | Frames and implements monetary policy for price stability + growth |
| Sole issuer of currency | Issues notes ≥ ₹2 (coins and ₹1 note by GoI) |
| Banker's bank | Holds banks' reserves, settles claims, **lender of last resort** |
| Banker to government | Manages accounts and **public debt** (G-secs) |
| Custodian of forex | Manages reserves and the rupee under **FEMA (1999)** |
| Regulator & supervisor | Oversees commercial/cooperative banks and **NBFCs** |
| Developmental role | Financial inclusion, digital payments (UPI, BBPS) |

## Terms explained

- **Statutory body** — a body created by an Act of Parliament (the RBI Act, 1934), not by the Constitution.
- **Nationalisation** — transfer of ownership from private hands to the government (RBI, 1 Jan 1949).
- **Lender of last resort** — the RBI gives emergency funds to a bank in crisis when no one else will.
- **G-secs** — government securities (bonds the government issues to borrow).

## TL;DR

- RBI Act passed 1934; RBI began operations 1 April 1935; nationalised 1 January 1949; HQ Mumbai.
- Central Board appointed by GoI for a four-year term; Governor + up to four Deputy Governors.
- RBI is the sole issuer of currency notes; coins and the ₹1 note are issued by the Government of India.
- As banker's bank it is the lender of last resort; as banker to government it manages public debt.
- Forex reserves are managed under FEMA 1999; RBI also regulates banks and NBFCs.

As banker's bank it is the lender of last resort; as banker to government it manages public debt.

Current RBI Governor (Sep 2026): Sanjay Malhotra.

items.title: Monetary Policy Tools & the LAF Corridor
items.body:
## In one line

**Monetary policy tools** are the levers the RBI uses to control how much money and credit flow in the economy. Examiners love the repo/CRR/SLR definitions and the current policy-rate values.

## Quantitative (general) tools

- **Repo rate** — rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks against G-secs; introduced under the **LAF in 2000**. Raise → curb inflation; cut → spur growth.
- **Reverse repo / SDF** — the **Standing Deposit Facility (2022)** replaced the fixed reverse repo as the LAF **floor**; absorbs surplus liquidity **without collateral**.
- **MSF (2011)** — banks borrow above the repo at a **penal rate** (LAF ceiling); the **Bank Rate** is aligned with it.
- **CRR** — cash reserves kept **with the RBI** (earns no interest).
- **SLR** — liquid assets (cash/gold/G-secs) held by the **bank itself**.
- **OMO (1992)** — buy G-secs = inject liquidity; sell = absorb. **MSS (2004)** sterilises capital inflows.

## Policy rates — as of October 2026

| Rate | Value |
|---|---|
| Policy repo rate | **5.50%** |
| SDF (corridor floor) | 5.25% |
| MSF / Bank Rate (ceiling) | 5.75% |
| CRR | 3.00% |
| SLR | 18.00% |

The LAF corridor is symmetric: **SDF (repo − 0.25) < repo < MSF (repo + 0.25)**.

## Terms explained

- **LAF** — Liquidity Adjustment Facility: the window (since 2000) through which the RBI lends (repo) or absorbs (SDF) money overnight.
- **Repo rate** — the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against G-secs.
- **CRR** — Cash Reserve Ratio: cash banks must keep with the RBI (no interest).
- **SLR** — Statutory Liquidity Ratio: liquid assets (cash/gold/G-secs) a bank keeps with itself.
- **Sterilisation** — mopping up extra money from foreign inflows (via OMO sales / MSS).

## TL;DR

- Repo rate introduced under the LAF in 2000; OMO began 1992; MSS 2004; MSF 2011.
- SDF (2022) is the LAF floor and absorbs liquidity without collateral; MSF is the penal ceiling.
- CRR is cash held with the RBI (no interest); SLR is liquid assets held by the bank itself.
- As of Oct 2026: repo 5.50%, SDF 5.25%, MSF/Bank Rate 5.75%, CRR 3.00%, SLR 18.00%.
- OMO buy/MSS absorb-issue are used to inject or drain systemic liquidity.

items.title: MPC & Inflation Targeting
items.body:
## In one line

The **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** is the six-member body that fixes the repo rate to keep inflation near a 4% target. It is asked for its composition, voting and the inflation band.

## Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)

- Established in **2016** via an amendment to the **RBI Act, 1934** (Section 45ZB), shifting from a Governor-centric to a committee model.
- **Six members** = 3 RBI (Governor as Chair + Deputy Governor for monetary policy + one RBI officer) and **3 external experts** appointed by the GoI.
- Meets **at least 4 times a year** (about once every two months); **quorum 4**; each member one vote; the **Governor has a casting vote** in a tie.

## Flexible inflation targeting

- India targets **CPI inflation of 4% with a ±2% tolerance band (2%–6%)**.
- The target is set by the Government in consultation with the RBI and **reviewed every five years**.
- CPI is compiled by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**.

## Terms explained

- **MPC** — Monetary Policy Committee: the six-member panel that votes on the repo rate.
- **Casting vote** — the extra vote the Governor uses to break a 3–3 tie.
- **Flexible inflation targeting** — a legal promise to keep CPI inflation at 4%, allowing a 2%–6% band.
- **CPI** — Consumer Price Index: measures retail price rise, compiled by the NSO.

## TL;DR

- MPC established 2016 under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934.
- Six members: 3 from RBI (Governor chairs) + 3 government-appointed external experts.
- MPC meets at least four times a year; quorum four; Governor holds the casting vote.
- Inflation target: 4% CPI with a ±2% band (2%–6%), reviewed every five years.
- CPI (the target measure) is compiled by the NSO.

items.title: Money Supply & the Money Multiplier
items.body:
## In one line

**Money supply** is the total money circulating in the economy (measured as M0–M4), and the **money multiplier** shows how a small base of reserve money expands into much larger bank deposits. Asked for aggregate definitions and a simple multiplier sum.

## Monetary aggregates (RBI classification)

| Aggregate | Composition |
|---|---|
| **M0** (reserve / high-powered money) | Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI |
| **M1** (narrow money) | Currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI |
| **M2** | M1 + savings deposits with post-office savings banks |
| **M3** (broad money) | M1 + time deposits with banks |
| **M4** | M3 + total post-office deposits |

- Liquidity decreases from M1 → M4; **M3** is the most-watched 'broad money'.

## Money multiplier

- **Money multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio** (simple case). Example: RR 20% → multiplier = 1/0.20 = **5**.
- It captures how a small rise in reserve money (M0) expands total deposits through lending and re-deposit.
- Inverse relationship with the reserve ratio; a higher **currency-to-deposit ratio** or cash leakage lowers it.

## Terms explained

- **M0 (reserve/high-powered money)** — currency plus banks' deposits with the RBI.
- **M3 (broad money)** — M1 plus time (fixed) deposits; the most-watched measure.
- **Reserve ratio** — the share of deposits a bank must hold back (CRR + SLR).
- **Money multiplier** — how many rupees of deposits each rupee of reserve money creates (= 1 ÷ reserve ratio).

## TL;DR

- M0 = high-powered/reserve money; M1 = narrow money; M3 = broad money (M1 + time deposits).
- Liquidity falls from M1 to M4; M3 is the key 'broad money' aggregate.
- Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; RR 20% gives a multiplier of 5.
- The multiplier has an inverse relationship with the reserve ratio.
- A higher currency-to-deposit ratio or cash leakage reduces the actual multiplier.
keyPoints: M0 = high-powered/reserve money; M1 = narrow money; M3 = broad money (M1 + time deposits).
Liquidity falls from M1 to M4; M3 is the key 'broad money' aggregate.
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; RR 20% gives a multiplier of 5.
The multiplier has an inverse relationship with the reserve ratio.
A higher currency-to-deposit ratio or cash leakage reduces the actual multiplier.
items.mnemonic: Broad-to-narrow: M1 is 'lively' (liquid), M3 adds time deposits, M4 adds all post-office money.

items.title: Banking Structure, Nationalisation & NPA Management
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains how India's **banks are classified**, the history of **nationalisation/merger**, and the tools used to recover **bad loans (NPAs)**. Asked for bank types, the 1969/1980/2020 milestones and SARFAESI/IBC.

## Classification of banks

- **Scheduled banks** are listed in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934** and can borrow from the RBI; **non-scheduled banks** are not.
- **Scheduled commercial banks**: public sector, private sector, foreign, **RRBs**, and **small finance banks**.
- Newer categories: **Small Finance Banks** (financial inclusion) and **Payments Banks** (deposits + payments, but **cannot lend or issue credit cards**).

## Nationalisation & consolidation

| Event | Year | Number |
|---|---|---|
| First nationalisation | 1969 | 14 banks |
| Second nationalisation | 1980 | 6 banks |
| Mega-merger | 2020 | 10 → 4 PSBs |

## Managing NPAs

- **SARFAESI Act, 2002** — recover secured loans without court intervention.
- **IBC, 2016** — time-bound insolvency resolution via the NCLT.
- **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA)** — RBI curbs on weak banks (capital/asset-quality triggers).
- **Priority-Sector Lending** — 40% of adjusted net bank credit to agriculture, MSMEs, weaker sections.

## Terms explained

- **Scheduled bank** — a bank listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934.
- **NPA (non-performing asset)** — a loan on which repayment is overdue beyond 90 days.
- **SARFAESI (2002)** — lets banks seize and sell a defaulter's secured assets without going to court.
- **IBC (2016)** — Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: time-bound resolution of defaults via the NCLT.
- **PCA** — Prompt Corrective Action: RBI curbs on a weak bank.

## TL;DR

- Scheduled banks are in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934; RRBs are scheduled commercial banks.
- Payments banks take deposits and offer payments but cannot lend or issue credit cards.
- Bank nationalisation: 14 banks in 1969, 6 in 1980; 2020 mega-merger cut 10 PSBs to 4.
- SARFAESI 2002 enables recovery of secured loans without courts; IBC 2016 gives time-bound insolvency.
- PCA imposes RBI restrictions on weak banks; PSL target is 40% of adjusted net bank credit.

items.title: Financial Markets, Inflation & Other Regulators
items.body:
## In one line

This note covers India's **financial markets**, the **types of inflation** and the **non-banking regulators** (SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA). Asked for money-vs-capital market, core-vs-headline inflation and which body regulates what.

## Financial markets

- **Money market** — short-term (≤1 year) instruments: T-bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, call money.
- **Capital market** — long-term equity and debt; split into **primary** (new issues/IPOs) and **secondary** (trading on NSE/BSE).
- **SEBI (1992)** regulates securities; **RBI** oversees the money market; the **FSDC** coordinates across regulators.
- **Lending-rate benchmarks:** the **MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate, 2016)** replaced the base rate to improve transparency and faster transmission of policy-rate cuts; new floating loans now use an **external benchmark (EBLR, e.g. repo-linked)**.

## Inflation — types & measures

- **Demand-pull** ('too much money chasing too few goods') vs **cost-push** (rising input costs) vs **structural** inflation.
- **Headline CPI** includes all items; **core inflation** excludes volatile food and fuel.
- Measures: **CPI** (compiled by NSO), **WPI** (Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT), GDP deflator, PPI.
- The **Phillips curve** shows the short-run inverse inflation–unemployment trade-off.

## Other regulators & inclusion

- **IRDAI (Act 1999)** — insurance regulator; **PFRDA** — pension regulator overseeing the **NPS** and **Atal Pension Yojana (APY)**.
- **PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014)** anchored the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) for direct benefit transfer.

## Terms explained

- **Money market** — market for short-term funds (one year or less).
- **Capital market** — market for long-term equity and debt.
- **Primary vs secondary market** — new issues (IPOs) vs trading of existing securities.
- **Core inflation** — the price trend after removing volatile food and fuel.
- **SEBI / IRDAI / PFRDA** — regulators of securities / insurance / pensions.

## TL;DR

- Money market = short-term (≤1 yr) instruments; capital market = long-term equity/debt.
- MCLR (2016) is the transparency-focused lending benchmark that replaced the base rate; new loans use an external benchmark (EBLR).
- Primary market issues new securities (IPOs); secondary market trades existing ones on NSE/BSE.
- SEBI (1992) regulates securities; CPI is compiled by NSO, WPI by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT).
- Core inflation excludes food and fuel; headline CPI includes all items.

items.title: Digital Payments — NPCI, UPI & the Digital Rupee
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains India's **digital-payments system** — the NPCI, UPI, card/transfer networks and the Digital Rupee. Asked heavily as current affairs: who runs UPI, latest volumes and the CBDC pilots.

## NPCI & its products

- **NPCI** (2008) is the not-for-profit umbrella body for retail payments, promoted by the **RBI and IBA** under the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.
- Flagship products: **RuPay** (domestic card network, 2012), **IMPS** (2010), **UPI** (2016) and **Bharat BillPay/BBPS** (interoperable bill payments).

## Fund-transfer systems

| System | Operator | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| RTGS | RBI | Real-time, large-value (≥₹2 lakh); 24x7 since Dec 2020 |
| NEFT | RBI | Batch retail transfer, no minimum; 24x7 since Dec 2019 |
| IMPS | NPCI | 24x7 instant mobile transfer (2010) |
| UPI | NPCI | Instant VPA-based P2P/P2M (2016), interoperable |

## UPI — scale (verified Sep 2026)

- Launched 2016; **completed 10 years in August 2026**.
- **August 2025: ~20 billion transactions worth ~₹25 lakh crore** in a single month.
- **FY 2025-26 value ≈ ₹314 lakh crore**; India ≈ half of the world's real-time digital payments.
- From **14 Sep 2026**, no charges on UPI payments up to ₹2,000 and on RuPay debit cards.

## Newer instruments

- **e-RUPI** (2021) — prepaid, purpose-specific e-voucher (QR/SMS), needs no account or app at the beneficiary's end.
- **Digital Rupee (e₹, CBDC)** — RBI's sovereign digital currency; **wholesale pilot 1 Nov 2022**, **retail pilot 1 Dec 2022**.
- **UPI global** — linked with Singapore's **PayNow (2023)**; accepted in UAE, France, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius (via NPCI International Payments Ltd).
- **Payments banks** — RBI 2014 guidelines (Nachiket Mor Committee); deposits up to ₹2 lakh; no lending or credit cards.

## Terms explained

- **NPCI** — National Payments Corporation of India: the not-for-profit umbrella that runs retail payments.
- **UPI** — Unified Payments Interface: instant bank-to-bank payment using a virtual address.
- **VPA** — Virtual Payment Address, e.g. name@bank, used instead of account numbers.
- **CBDC / Digital Rupee (e₹)** — digital cash issued by the RBI; it is legal tender.
- **e-RUPI** — a prepaid, purpose-specific e-voucher sent as a QR code or SMS.

## TL;DR

- NPCI (2008), promoted by RBI & IBA under the PSS Act 2007, runs RuPay (2012), IMPS (2010), UPI (2016) and BBPS.
- RTGS (≥₹2 lakh) and NEFT are RBI systems, both now 24x7; IMPS and UPI are NPCI systems.
- UPI launched 2016, completed 10 years in Aug 2026; Aug 2025 saw ~20 billion transactions worth ~₹25 lakh crore.
- UPI value reached ~₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26; from 14 Sep 2026 no charges on UPI up to ₹2,000.
- e-RUPI (2021) is a prepaid purpose-specific voucher needing no account/app at the recipient's end.

items.title: For Mains — RBI, Banking & Financial Markets
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains, RBI/banking is examined not as definitions but as a **policy debate**: can monetary policy and banking reform deliver price stability, resource mobilisation and inclusive growth together? (Serves Paper-4 clauses M4-1 and M4-2.)

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | Supply-side inflation (food/fuel), legacy NPAs, slow transmission, thin credit in rural areas |
| Features | FIT framework (4% ±2% CPI), LAF corridor, MPC, SARFAESI/IBC, JAM-led inclusion |
| Significance | Anchors expectations, mobilises savings, channels credit to productive sectors |
| Impact | Lower inflation volatility; wider formal credit via UPI/Jan Dhan |
| Criticism / limits | Weak against cost-push shocks; incomplete transmission; regional credit gaps |
| Way forward | Supply-side management, faster EBLR transmission, governance reform, deeper inclusion |

## Data / committees / reports to quote

- **FIT framework** — statutory since the 2016 RBI Act amendment; **4% CPI ±2%** target.
- **Policy corridor (Oct 2026):** repo 5.50%, SDF 5.25%, MSF/Bank Rate 5.75%, CRR 3.00%, SLR 18.00%.
- **Urjit Patel Committee (2014)** recommended inflation targeting; **Nachiket Mor Committee** shaped payments/small-finance banks.
- **IBC, 2016** and **SARFAESI, 2002** for NPA resolution; **PCA** framework for weak banks.
- **PMJDY (2014)** + **UPI** (~₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26) for financial inclusion.

## AP angle

For an agrarian, coastal state like **Andhra Pradesh**, transmission shapes the cost of **crop loans, MSME and aquaculture credit**; **RRBs (AP Grameena Vikas Bank)**, SHG-bank linkage and Jan Dhan accounts anchor rural credit and DBT.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** cite the 2025–26 rate-cut cycle (repo cut to 5.50%) as monetary easing to support growth.
- **Quote:** monetary policy is 'a blunt instrument against supply-side inflation'.
- **Diagram idea:** draw the LAF corridor (SDF < repo < MSF) or the JAM trinity triangle.
keyPoints: Mains frames RBI/banking as a policy debate on price stability, resource mobilisation and inclusive growth (M4-1, M4-2).
Use the dimensions table: causes, features, significance, impact, criticism, way forward.
Quote FIT (2016, 4% ±2%), the Oct 2026 corridor, Urjit Patel & Nachiket Mor committees, IBC/SARFAESI, PMJDY/UPI.
Key limits: weak against supply-side inflation, incomplete transmission, regional credit gaps.
AP angle: RRBs, SHG-bank linkage and Jan Dhan underpin rural credit and DBT in AP.
